title: Life problems and self-enquiry: what can you explore?
description: Explore confidence, overthinking, anger, guilt, grief, relationships, uncertainty, and spiritual clarity through the philosophy of shared Creator identity.
intro: This philosophy addresses how we meet life's difficulties by remembering our shared Creator identity within the game of experiences. Choose a concern below to find clarity, a relatable everyday example, and a question for self-enquiry.
scope: These are concerns discussed in the philosophy and applications of its teaching, not a promise to solve every external problem. Recognition is intended to change our relationship with experience; practical action, learning, protection, and appropriate support remain part of life.
homeLink: Explore the full guide to life’s difficulties
healthLimit: For depression, persistent anxiety, sleep problems, fatigue, or illness, spiritual enquiry can accompany appropriate healthcare. This philosophy is not a treatment, a diagnosis, or a promise to prevent illness. Sleep, vitality, and immunity were discussed as hoped-for benefits, not established outcomes of this teaching.
worldLimit: Poverty, job insecurity, harm to nature, and unsafe technology also require practical resources, cooperation, and safeguards. The Beautiful World vision gives these concerns a direction for compassionate enquiry and constructive action.
confidenceTitle: Self-enquiry for confidence, self-worth and fear of failure
confidenceDescription: Explore low confidence, comparison, rejection, and fear of failure through shared Creator identity. Discover a fresh perspective, a practical job example, and a reflection for daily life.
overthinkingTitle: Overthinking, worry and uncertainty: a self-enquiry guide
overthinkingDescription: Explore repeated thoughts, worry, and uncertainty through the understanding of the designed game. Discover an everyday example and ways to participate with peace instead of forced certainty.

categories.title: Difficult emotions and self-judgment
categories.concerns: Anger · Resentment · Guilt · Shame · Self-blame · Emotional pain
categories.aliases: angry anger resentment resentful guilty ashamed blame hurt
categories.example: Suppose a hurtful remark leaves you angry. In this understanding, both people share the one Creator identity; anger is an experience within the game, not your whole identity. You can acknowledge the hurt, pause before replying, and say clearly what is unacceptable. Remembering connection does not require suppressing anger or tolerating harm.
categories.reflection: What was hurt, and what response or boundary is needed now?

categories.title: Loss, sadness and loneliness
categories.concerns: Sadness · Grief · Loneliness · Disappointment · Fear of death · Feeling overwhelmed
categories.aliases: lonely alone loneliness grieving bereavement bereaved sad overwhelmed death disappointment
categories.example: An evening alone after a loss may bring grief or loneliness. Deep sadness and compassion can coexist with steady inner peace. Remembering the shared Creator does not mean forcing yourself to feel joyful or denying the person you miss. Give the feeling space, reach out to someone you trust, and care for one simple need. Healing takes time.
categories.reflection: Can you give this feeling space while remembering that a painful scene is not the whole of who you are?

categories.title: Relationships, family and boundaries
categories.concerns: Family conflict · Blame · Hurtful conversations · Mistrust · Difficulty setting boundaries · Responding to wrongdoing
categories.aliases: family conflict trust distrust mistrust boundary boundaries wrongdoing argument
categories.example: After a family argument, the urge to prove who is right can overshadow the people involved. Remember the shared Creator, listen without humiliation, and help with what is reasonably possible. Name the actual disagreement, acknowledge your part, and make a clear request. A boundary can coexist with care; another person’s agreement cannot be forced.
categories.reflection: What needs understanding, what needs repair, and what needs a firm boundary?

categories.title: Money, status and attachment
categories.concerns: Attachment to money · Status anxiety · Greed · Jealousy · Fear of financial loss · Conflict over possessions
categories.aliases: jealous envy envious jealousy greedy greed money finances financial attachment status
categories.example: A friend’s success may stir jealousy, or a disagreement over money may threaten a relationship. Money and status are merely small parts of the creation; they cannot enlarge or diminish our shared Creator identity. Notice the comparison without self-condemnation. Care for your practical needs and agreements, while recognizing that possessions do not define your worth.
categories.reflection: What practical need deserves attention, and what comparison are you treating as a measure of who you are?
